API 510 vs API 570: Pressure Vessel vs Piping Inspector [2026 Guide]

API 510 and API 570 certifications offer distinct career paths in equipment inspection. This guide explains the credential differences, salary expectations, responsibilities, and which path suits your career goals.

By Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III · 2026-03-21T00:00:00Z

Overview of Both Certifications

API 510 (Pressure Vessel Inspector) and API 570 (Piping Inspector) certifications represent two specialized pathways in industrial equipment inspection. Both are issued by the American Petroleum Institute (API) and are respected globally across oil, gas, chemical, and power generation industries. API 510 focuses on stationary pressure vessels, storage tanks, and heat exchangers. API 570 focuses on in-service piping systems and pipeline integrity.

API 510 certification was established in 1935 and covers pressure vessel inspection under the API 510 standard. API 570 emerged from piping inspection needs in the 1960s and now covers in-service piping inspection per API 570 standard. Both certifications require demonstrated knowledge through rigorous examinations and documented field experience.

API 510 inspectors typically work for refinery vessel operations, petrochemical plants, and insurance companies authorizing vessel continued service. API 570 inspectors focus on piping reliability within operating plants, supporting corrosion management programs and asset integrity initiatives. Career progression differs significantly between the two paths.

When to Pursue API 510 Certification

API 510 is ideal if you prefer specialized focus on vessel integrity and thermodynamic equipment. Pressure vessels require understanding of design codes (ASME Section VIII), material properties, and complex failure modes. If detailed engineering knowledge appeals to you more than broad asset management, API 510 aligns better.

Refinery positions heavily favor API 510 inspectors. A typical refinery with 50+ pressure vessels (reactors, fractionators, heat exchangers) employs 2-4 API 510 inspectors managing vessel integrity programs, coordinating turnarounds, and ensuring regulatory compliance. Refinery positions offer stable employment with excellent benefits and salary advancement.

Insurance company inspectors (third-party authorized inspectors) are typically API 510 certified. Insurance companies authorize vessel continued operation and require deep understanding of ASME code compliance, material degradation, and safe operating envelopes. Third-party work offers excellent salary ($80,000-$120,000) and geographic variety.

Petrochemical plants with complex reactor systems (hydrocracking, hydrotreating, polymerization) require API 510 expertise. Reactor vessel expertise directly impacts process yield and safety. API 510 inspectors in complex chemistry plants command premium salaries ($90,000-$110,000) due to specialized knowledge.

Career stability in API 510 is good long-term. Even as refineries consolidate, legacy vessels require ongoing inspection. Remaining refinery operations and specialty chemical plants need experienced API 510 inspectors. Certified inspectors (age 55+) often stay employed longer than uncertified technicians.

When to Pursue API 570 Certification

API 570 suits you if you prefer systems-level thinking and enjoy managing complex piping networks across plants. Piping systems are distributed across entire facilities, requiring broad perspective. If you want impact across multiple equipment systems rather than deep focus on one equipment type, API 570 offers more scope.

Reliability and asset integrity programs strongly favor API 570 inspectors. Modern plants implement Risk-Based Inspection (RBI) per API 579, focusing resources on highest-risk piping. API 570 inspectors lead these initiatives, directly protecting equipment and improving operational efficiency. Salary advancement is rapid in growing RBI programs ($75,000-$105,000).

Plant-based positions favor API 570. Operating plants employ 1-3 API 570 inspectors managing thousands of miles of piping. Corrosion management programs, ultrasonic thickness (UT) inspection campaigns, and failure analysis fall under API 570 responsibility. Plant-based work offers stability with minimal travel, appealing to those preferring single-location employment.

Oil and gas pipeline operations increasingly require API 570 expertise. Pipeline operators managing high-pressure transmission lines employ API 570 inspectors for integrity management, inspection planning, and regulatory reporting. Pipeline positions offer excellent salary ($75,000-$105,000) and career specialization.

Consulting and engineering firms value API 570 inspectors for risk assessment, inspection program development, and technical support. Consulting offers variety and learning opportunities, with salaries reaching $80,000-$120,000 including benefits. Consulting roles are well-suited for career changers from operations.

Cost Comparison

Exam Fees: Both API 510 and API 570 exams cost $600-$750 per attempt through API (2026 pricing). Re-exam fees are identical. Test preparation courses cost $2,500-$4,500 through providers like ProCert Training, Quest Training, and Offshore Compliance Institute.

Certification Maintenance: Both certifications require recertification every 3 years. Recertification costs $300-$400 and requires documented continuing education (40 hours per 3-year cycle for API 510; 50 hours for API 570). Annual maintenance cost approximately $100-$150 per certification.

Experience Documentation: Both paths require verified work experience. Obtaining reference letters and experience verification costs minimal; however, time investment is significant (10-20 hours for comprehensive documentation).

Career Advancement Cost: API 510 inspectors typically advance through refinery/facility promotions or third-party inspector transitions (requiring no additional exam). API 570 inspectors can transition to Certified Reliability Professional (CRP) through ASNT path, requiring additional training ($3,000-$5,000).

Total 3-Year Cycle Cost: API 510: exam $600, recert $300, continuing education $400 = $1,300 over 3 years. API 570: exam $600, recert $400, continuing education $500 = $1,500 over 3 years.

Salary Comparison (2026)

Entry-Level Inspector (years 0-3): API 510: $60,000-$75,000 base; API 570: $55,000-$70,000 base. Entry-level positions often require 5 years experience under mentorship, so "entry" is relative. Starting positions typically include plant operator roles leading to inspector track.

Certified Inspector (years 3-8): API 510: $75,000-$95,000 base + benefits; API 570: $70,000-$85,000 base + benefits. Field positions add 20-30% for travel and on-call work. API 510 field inspectors earn $85,000-$110,000.

Senior Inspector/Supervisor (years 8+): API 510: $90,000-$130,000 including third-party inspector roles; API 570: $85,000-$120,000 including asset management positions. Senior positions include overtime and on-call differentials adding 15-25%.

Geographic Variation: Gulf Coast refinery positions (Houston, Corpus Christi, Lake Charles) pay 10-15% premium. West Coast positions (San Francisco, Los Angeles) pay 15-20% premium. Midwest positions are typically 5-10% below national average.

Experience Premium: Each year of experience beyond 5 years adds approximately $1,500-$2,500 annually to salary. Inspectors with 15+ years command $110,000-$140,000+ in refinery environments.

Job Market and Career Outlook

API 510 Outlook: 2026 refinery market shows consolidation with reduced new construction. Existing refinery operations maintain steady demand for API 510 inspectors. Retirements of aging inspectors create openings despite fewer new positions. Job security for certified inspectors is excellent; 40-50 active positions nationally for experienced inspectors.

API 570 Outlook: Growing asset integrity programs drive strong demand. 2026 pipeline safety regulations increase inspection requirements, benefiting API 570 inspectors. Chemical plant expansions favor piping specialists. 100-150 active positions nationally with 20% annual growth in asset management focus.

Hybrid Certifications: Many senior inspectors obtain both API 510 and API 570, commanding salaries $120,000-$150,000. Dual certification requires 2-3 additional years of specific experience but dramatically improves career opportunities and advancement speed.

Which Certification Path Should You Choose?

Choose API 510 If: You prefer depth over breadth, enjoy detailed engineering knowledge, want focused expertise in vessel design and materials, prefer field travel and variety, or are drawn to refinery operations.

Choose API 570 If: You prefer broad systems thinking, enjoy corrosion management and failure analysis, want plant-based work with stability, prefer minimal travel, or are interested in reliability engineering and asset management careers.

Optimal Strategy: Many successful inspectors pursue API 570 first (higher job availability, more accessible entry paths), then add API 510 after 3-4 years. Dual certification positions you for senior management roles ($120,000-$150,000) and provides career flexibility across refinery and plant operations.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Can I get API 510 without 5 years experience? A: No. API 510 exam requires documented 5 years pressure vessel inspection or engineering experience. Experience must occur within 10 years of exam date. Entry-level progression: plant operator (1-2 years) → inspection technician under API 510 mentor (2-3 years) → eligible for exam.

Q: What's the API 570 exam pass rate? A: Approximately 65% of candidates pass the API 570 exam. First-time pass rate is about 60%; repeat exam rate increases to 75-80%. Thorough preparation through formal courses increases pass probability to 75-85%.

Q: Do I need both API 510 and API 570? A: Most inspectors specialize in one certification. Dual certification is valuable for career advancement (positions like Inspection Manager or Reliability Engineer favor dual-certified candidates). Single certification is sufficient for most field positions. Budget 3-4 additional years experience between certifications.

Q: How much travel is required for API 510 inspectors? A: Third-party inspectors travel 50-70% (field assignment-dependent). In-house refinery inspectors travel 10-20% for turnarounds and specialized inspections. Travel expectations vary by employer and position type.

Q: Can I work as an API 510 inspector with only 5 years experience? A: Yes, though advancement is limited. Most employers prefer API 510 inspectors with 7+ years experience for independent assignment. With 5 years, expect to work under senior inspector supervision for the first 1-2 years.

Q: What NDT certifications complement API 510/570? A: ASNT Level II or III in UT (ultrasonic), RT (radiography), and MT (magnetic particle) certifications enhance inspector credentials. UT certification is most valuable (70% of inspections use UT). Combined ASNT certifications increase salary 10-15%.

Q: How often must I recertify? A: Both API 510 and API 570 recertification is every 3 years. Recertification requires 40-50 hours continuing education plus recertification exam ($300-$400). Recertification maintains credential value and demonstrates current knowledge.

Q: Is API 510 or 570 more recognized globally? A: Both certifications are respected internationally. API 510 is particularly valued in Middle East and Asia refinery operations. API 570 is standard in European pipeline operations. Single certification (API 510 or 570) is sufficient for international work.

Q: What's the salary difference between certified and uncertified inspectors? A: Certified API 510/570 inspectors earn 30-40% more than uncertified inspection technicians. Uncertified technicians earn $45,000-$60,000; certified earn $65,000-$95,000. Certification is the primary salary driver in inspection careers.

Q: Can I transition from API 510 to API 570 mid-career? A: Yes. Cross-certification is common after 5+ years in one discipline. You must document 5 years experience in the new discipline. Time overlap (experience in both vessels and piping) accelerates cross-certification path. Total 3-year timeframe is typical.
